subject: english-literature
title: Allusion and Echo
welcome_lead: Intertextuality is the third area of exploration. Every text speaks with and against other texts — allusions enrich, parody critiques, adaptation reinvents.
meta_desc: English Literature: intertextuality, allusion, parody and literary echo.
final_note: Literature is a long conversation. Join it carefully.

concepts.def: An indirect reference to another text, figure or event.
Comic imitation of another work that exaggerates its features.

Harold Bloom's term for the inescapable debt of writers to predecessors.
Bloom's theory that strong writers struggle against the shadow of precursors.

walkthroughs.body_html: Parody mocks its source; pastiche celebrates it. Jane Austen's Northanger Abbey parodies the gothic novel. Zadie Smith's On Beauty pastiches Forster's Howards End.
Bloom argues every strong poet rewrites their precursors through six revisionary ratios. Reading Wordsworth without Milton in mind misses the wrestling beneath.
An echo can be tonal as well as verbal. The opening of Beloved — '124 was spiteful' — echoes biblical incantation. Train your ear for inherited cadences.
